transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-22
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Dr. Evelyn Martin (Sequoia CTO), Janelle Ortega (Lead ML), Samir Patel (Platform), Nina Lowe (Procurement)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be incomplete):
- Reviewed POC benchmark results comparing Redwood inference to their incumbent provider (IncumbentX).
- Redwood shows lower p50 latency and comparable throughput after batching/kv cache tuning; some p99 spikes remain during long-context traces.
- Action items: share raw logs, run dedicated latency debugging session, confirm SLA acceptance.

---- Transcript ----
[00:00] Alex (AE): okay hi everyone thanks for hopping on, we wanted to do a quick run through of the lab results from last week's run and, um, go over a few tuning knobs we flipped. can you all see my screen?
[00:12] Evelyn (CTO): yes we can, thanks alex. afternoon all. excited to see the numbers.
[00:17] Priya (SE): hey, quick note i pulled the aggregated CSVs into the sheet link i sent in the chat a minute ago, should help when we reference the p95/p99.
[00:27] Janelle (Lead ML): i got it, opening now. i noticed the baseline has a 50ms lower p50 in one run but then p99 is worse — curious how you measured.
[00:35] Marco (SE): yeah the baseline here is IncumbentX that sequoia has been running, right? we're comparing the same model family but with our quantization and continuous KV caching on.
[00:45] Samir (Platform): correct, we tried to keep token limits and concurrency similar, but their infra uses heavier pre-warming.
[00:52] Alex: exactly. quick context: workload used was customer chat assistant template, mean seq len ~250 tokens, bursts up to 1k tokens for some docs. concurrent lanes set to 40 in the Redwood Dedicated pool during the test.
[01:05] Evelyn: ok, can you walk through latency numbers topline?
[01:10] Priya: sure. p50 across requests for Redwood in run A was 85ms vs incumbent 132ms; p95 was 240ms vs 275ms; p99 was 1.2s vs 0.9s — so we beat them on median and p95 but saw p99 regression.
[01:26] Janelle: that p99 jump is concerning, 1.2s from 0.9s would be noticeable. do you have a breakdown by request type?
[01:34] Marco: yes, the spike correlates with long-context recalls where KV cache misses and large attention windows kicked in. our continuous batching also introduces occasional head-of-line latency if a very long request enters the queue.
[01:45] Priya: also worth noting transcription: during heavy KV eviction scenarios for a subset of requests we saw an extra 300-400ms for KV rehydration on the nodes that were busy. i think that's the p99 edge case.
[01:55] Samir: hmm is that something we can tune in Redwood or is that inherent to the model/quantization?
[02:01] Priya: there are multiple levers — we can increase prefix cache retention (reduce evictions), reduce batch timeout for latency-sensitive endpoints, or route long-context requests to a variant optimized for long sequences — e.g., a larger memory instance or a different kernel selection.
[02:18] Evelyn: at what cost tradeoff? our procurement will push back if costs spike.
[02:23] Alex: good question. we prepared a simple cost delta: for the test run matching throughput, Redwood average token cost estimate was ~12% lower than IncumbentX. if we reduce batch timeout from 20ms to 5ms to remove H.O.L latency it'll increase per-token CPU load and raise cost by ~6-8% in the scenario. increasing cache retention increases memory footprint and could require an extra slot at high concurrency, approx +10% cost. but those are knobs we can tune per route.
[02:49] Janelle: can you share the spreadsheet numbers again? the cost model linked earlier i can't find the assumption for slot sizes.
[02:55] Marco: i'll re-share; main assumptions are vGPU equivalent to A100-80GB for Redwood Dedicated testbed, identical to what IncumbentX claimed they were using. but their real infra uses aggressive pre-warming which reduces latency at the expense of idle cost.
[03:11] Nina (Procurement): quick question from my side: for the pilot are we still on a month-to-month pricing or do we need to lock in a committed recurring slot to get those lower unit rates?
[03:19] Alex: pilot is month-to-month, you can spin up dedicated slots; committed reserved capacity discounts apply if you sign a 6-12 month commit. we can run this pilot without a commitment.
[03:27] Evelyn: thanks. back to performance — were the throughput numbers measured with synthetic traffic or replay?
[03:33] Priya: we used a blended replay from your production traces Samir provided plus synthetic high-concurrency bursts to stress the HTTP layer. sustained throughput with Redwood in the test was 1200 tokens/sec per slot under the modeled workload vs incumbent at ~1150 tokens/sec — so slightly better throughput for us.
[03:50] Samir: that's promising. did you observe any error rates or tail backpressure?
[03:55] Marco: error rates were low overall (~0.2% transient 5xx) and mainly during the longest bursts when we pushed concurrency above the tested SLO. we have traces for each 5xx event in the logs.
[04:06] Janelle: do those 5xx tie to memory OOMs or timeouts?
[04:10] Priya: mostly timeouts while waiting on downstream model shard—so increased latency cascades to auth timeouts in our test harness.
[04:16] Nina: any notes about data handling? compliance is important for us — we need retention and logs for audit.
[04:21] Alex: yes, per our conversations Redwood Private options exist for longer retention and control plane in VPC; we've also documented KMS integration for encryption at rest. we'll include the security doc link again.
[04:33] Evelyn: ok that's good. procurement will want SOC2 report and ISO certs.
[04:37] Alex: we are SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certified — i'll drop the cert pack into the workspace after the call.
[04:44] [05:00] (background cross talk)
[05:10] Priya: back to tuning, we tried three profiles in the run: default, low-latency, and cost-optimized. default had batching timeout 20ms, low-latency 5ms with smaller batch sizes, cost-optimized used more aggressive quantization and batch timeouts up to 50ms.
[05:25] Marco: in low-latency profile median latency dropped to 60ms but throughput per slot decreased about 10% — the tradeoff line. cost-optimized pushed per-token cost down 18% but p99 got worse for long-context.
[05:39] Janelle: interesting, did you try a hybrid: route short queries to low-latency profile and long ones to cost-optimized?
[05:46] Priya: yes we ran a routing policy in the final test: we classified by length <128 tokens to low-latency pool, >=128 to cost-optimized pool. that produced p50 ~70ms and p95 ~230ms and improved overall cost by 10% compared to default, while keeping p99 around 1.0s.
[06:05] Evelyn: that hybrid sounds promising — how much ops overhead to maintain two pools?
[06:09] Alex: minimal, the Redwood routing policy is config driven; you can do canary and A/B rollouts per route. ops overhead is mostly monitoring and minor capacity planning.
[06:18] Samir: curious about the p99 spike distribution — can you show an example trace?
[06:23] Priya: yes, pulling up a trace now — link pasted. (pause) here's a 1.18s trace: you can see a 420ms KV rehydrate step, then 300ms wait in queue due to a large request getting batched earlier. transcription in the logs labels some entries oddly — e.g., 'red wood' or 'red-wud' in a couple places, might be STT mislabels.
[06:43] Janelle: haha yeah i've seen that in other auto transcripts. can you annotate what fixes you recommend for that particular trace?
[06:48] Priya: for that trace: 1) bump prefix retention to reduce rehydrates on hot keys, 2) apply a slim route for requests with expected >700 tokens routing to long-context pool, 3) lower batch-window to 10ms for that particular route to reduce head-of-line. Those three changes should cut that tail by ~600-700ms.
[07:05] Evelyn: if we do all three are we still within your test cost envelope?
[07:09] Alex: net cost delta likely +4-6% on overall token cost given the mix from your traces, but it depends on fraction of long queries. if your traffic is 85% short queries cost uplift is negligible.
[07:20] Samir: we can share updated traffic distribution, expect about 20% long-context.
[07:24] Janelle: note — our product requires guaranteed p95 under 300ms for the UI flows. p99 we prefer sub-1s but it's less strict.
[07:33] Alex: that aligns with our hybrid results where p95 ~230ms and p99 ~1.0s after routing, so we can meet the p95 target.
[07:40] Marco: also want to call out that IncumbentX's pre-warming explains their better p99 in the baseline tests — they keep idle replications warm which reduces tail but increases cost. If Sequoia doesn't want reserve warm nodes, our routing/caching strategies get you similar p95 with lower cost.
[07:55] Nina: for procurement, we need clarity on SLA — what does Redwood guarantee for p95/p99?
[08:00] Alex: standard SLA covers uptime and latency SLOs are contractual per-tier. for Dedicated we can commit to 99th percentile latency caps for configured routes with penalties; we'll draft the matrix based on your agreed routes.
[08:13] Evelyn: great — can you include sample SLA language in the follow-up?
[08:16] Alex: yes will include.
[08:18] Priya: another note: we saw a sporadic regression tied to GC cycles on two nodes in the test harness; those were caused by a memory-heavy daemon (housekeeping job) collocated on the node. in production we'd isolate or pin housekeeping to different hosts.
[08:31] Samir: that's a good catch, we'll make sure infra team isn't running expensive batch jobs on service nodes.
[08:36] Janelle: about quantization — did cost-optimized profile use int4 or int8?
[08:40] Marco: cost-optimized used int8 with per-channel quantization; int4 was experimental and showed more variability in output quality for some prompts so we didn't include it in the official run.
[08:50] Janelle: any QA on semantic deltas when you used more aggressive quantization?
[08:54] Priya: yes we ran a 200 prompt eval; ROUGE/EM-like proxies showed <1.5% quality delta for int8; int4, where we tried it, trended 3-4% and had occasional hallucination patterns on certain domain entities. we can share eval results.
[09:09] Evelyn: we'll need those eval artifacts to sign off. can you share the prompt set?
[09:12] Alex: yes we'll push prompt set and evaluation outputs into the shared folder.
[09:16] [09:30] (brief silence as files are pasted)
[09:35] Nina: proc question — if we move to Redwood Private what is the onboarding timeline? we have compliance windows.
[09:41] Alex: typical Private deployment for a new customer is 6-8 weeks including network setup, KMS integration, and validation. there are accelerated paths if you take a supported appliance.
[09:49] Nina: ok noted.
[09:51] Samir: back to throughput — if we split traffic to two pools would that require double the slot count or will one slot handle both profiles?
[09:58] Marco: you can multiplex on the same pool but it's cleaner to allocate separate pools for predictable SLOs. if you keep a single pool, we rely on runtime priorities; this risks interference during bursts. separate pools are recommended when p95/p99 constraints are strict.
[10:16] Evelyn: cost delta for two pools vs one?
[10:20] Alex: two pools will require slightly more capacity headroom overall — estimate +12% capacity vs a single tuned pool, but it yields better isolation and easier SLA guarantees.
[10:28] Janelle: can you run one more targeted experiment: hybrid routing with low-latency pool sized for 1.25x short-query qps and a long-pool for the remainder, measure p99 for 24h?
[10:38] Priya: yes we can run that; we'll need the traffic tail file from Samir to replay a realistic 24h distribution.
[10:44] Samir: i'll send the sample later today.
[10:46] Alex: good, so new bench run is an action item. we'll schedule it for the 26th and share preliminary results on the 27th.
[10:55] (brief side chat about calendar availability)
[11:05] Priya: small practical: we observed one mislabeling in the trace where the profiler tagged a function 'kvcache-eject' as 'kvcache-eggz' in the STT; not a functional issue but might confuse automated parsers.
[11:16] Janelle: noted, we'll ignore that for now.
[11:18] Evelyn: any other risks to flag?
[11:21] Marco: main risks: tail latency for long-context requests (mitigatable), slight per-token cost uplift for low-latency profile, and the usual integration work for VPC/KMS.
[11:31] Nina: from cost/procurement view that seems manageable provided we get the SLA language and price model.
[11:36] Alex: we'll include a scenario-based price model: current pilot (month-to-month), 6-month reserved slot pricing, and committed reserved discount.
[11:44] Evelyn: ok let me summarize then next steps — (1) Redwood to share raw logs, benchmark CSV, and cost model by 2026-04-24; (2) Sequoia to share final traffic distribution and p95/p99 targets by 2026-04-25; (3) Redwood to run hybrid routing 24h replay test on 2026-04-26 and post results 2026-04-27; (4) Redwood to share SOC2/ISO certs and sample SLA language by 2026-04-24.
[12:12] Alex: yep that's correct. any other asks?
[12:16] Nina: procurement wants clarity on data retention windows for pilot logs — can you state default retention?
[12:22] Alex: default retention for pilot logs is 30 days; we can extend to 365 days on Private with KMS controls. we'll outline options in the follow-up doc.
[12:33] Samir: we'll get the traffic file today.
[12:36] Janelle: please also include the prompt evaluation artifacts for quantization checks.
[12:40] Alex: noted.
[12:42] Priya: final note — we'll propose the low-latency routing settings and a one-click config patch for you to try in staging before the 26th run.
[12:51] Evelyn: perfect. thanks everyone.
[12:54] Alex: thanks all, i'll follow up with the links and tasks.
[12:58] (meeting ends)
